title: Niagara-on-the-Lake — Discover Canada's Most Haunted & Beautiful Town
excerpt: Explore Niagara-on-the-Lake, a stunning 19th-century Canadian town known for wine, history, and thrilling nightly ghost tours just 1.5 hours from Toronto.
content:
Located about an hour and a half’s drive from Toronto in the Ontario wine region, Niagara-on-the-Lake was named one of the ’50 Most Beautiful Small Towns in the World’ in 2023 by the American travel magazine Condé Nast Traveler. Famed for its well-preserved 19th-century architecture, the town also holds the moniker of ‘Canada’s most haunted town,’ drawing crowds every October as Halloween approaches to take part in nightly ghost tours.

A Rebuilt Town Woven with Canadian History

The history of Niagara-on-the-Lake is deeply intertwined with early Canadian history. According to the Canadian Encyclopedia, Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe designated the area as the temporary capital of Upper Canada in 1792, and the legislature met here until the capital was moved to York (now Toronto) in 1796. During the War of 1812, American forces captured the town and Fort George in May 1813, burning the settlement down upon their withdrawal that December. The current streetscape was rebuilt by loyalist settlers following the war.

These reconstructed buildings are today the town’s greatest asset. The Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada recognizes Niagara-on-the-Lake for preserving the country’s finest collection of buildings constructed between 1815 and 1859, designating it a National Historic Site in 2004. Fort George, which served as a bastion defending Upper Canada against American attacks, now operates as a historic site showcasing wartime history.

Ghost Tours and Legendary Tales

The town’s spooky reputation stems from its long history. The Olde Angel Inn, one of the town’s prominent landmarks established around 1789, was burned during the War of 1812 and rebuilt in 1815. According to local lore popularized by the inn, Canadian militia Captain Colin Swayze delayed his retreat during the May 1813 American invasion to meet his lover and hid in an empty barrel in the inn’s cellar. Unfortunately, American soldiers thrust bayonets into potential hiding spots, taking his life. Legend has it his ghost still wanders the inn at night.

Ghost tours tracing these tales run nightly throughout October until Halloween, and on Friday and Saturday nights in November and December. Starting at the souvenir shop on 125A Queen Street, the 90-hour outdoor walking tour covers the Prince of Wales Hotel, the Royal George Theatre, the old apothecary, and the Olde Angel Inn. Operating in a traditional storytelling format without entering buildings, it leans closer to a history walk than a pure fright experience. The ‘most haunted town’ moniker is largely a reputation built by tour operators and the community rather than an official ranking.

A Fall Destination Blending Wine, Theater, and History

For visitors preferring history and scenery over ghost stories, the region offers plenty to explore. Known as the birthplace of modern Canadian wine, the area features dozens of wineries, including Chateau des Charmes on York Road, which offers tours and tastings. Strolling down Queen Street, lined with charming shops and cafes, leads visitors to the Shaw Festival theater, North America’s premier theater festival dedicated to the works of Irish playwright George Bernard Shaw. Founded in 1962, the summer festival stages over ten productions annually and attracts approximately 350,000 theatergoers.
